title: Why You Shouldn't Redirect Misbehavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the instinct to physically intervene and redirect students the moment misbehavior is spotted, arguing it invites arguments and defensiveness. He explains that correcting a student mid-misbehavior encourages them to explain away or justify their actions and puts the teacher at risk of losing composure. The deeper problem, he argues, is that immediate redirection prevents students from reflecting on their own mistakes, which reduces the odds they take real responsibility and increases the odds of repeat misbehavior. His alternative is to let the misbehavior play out fully, then approach only once it's finished and deliver a calm, brief consequence before walking away. He frames this approach as both less confrontational and more effective at curbing future misbehavior than in-the-moment correction.
points: Redirecting a student mid-misbehavior invites argument, justification, and a defensive reaction.
Immediate correction removes the student's chance to reflect and recognize their own mistake.
Letting misbehavior play out, then delivering the consequence afterward, produces less confrontation and more accountability.
A calm, brief, factual consequence statement followed by a quick exit avoids drawing the teacher into debate.
Redirection also risks the teacher losing their cool, since it interrupts their own teaching.
quotes: You catch a student in the act of misbehavior and you move in to redirect them.
Well, because it’s done while the student is in the act of misbehavior , it encourages an argumentative response.
You see, whenever you try to stop misbehavior while it’s occurring, you increase the likelihood of a confrontation—particularly with difficult students.
The chief reason for this is that redirection doesn’t allow your students to reflect on their mistakes.
It’s best to let the misbehavior play out , to continue with whatever you’re doing while keeping an eye on the student.
The calm clarity of the message, combined with your quick exit from the scene, causes the student to automatically contemplate their violation of class rules.
The best part, though, is that there is no confrontation, no resentment, and no added disruption to your teaching.
